summary: Researchers led by Mercedes Sotos-Prieto developed the MEDLIFE index to measure adherence to a Mediterranean lifestyle covering food, dietary habits, and physical activity, rest and social habits. In more than 110,000 UK participants followed for ten years, the lifestyle was feasible outside the Mediterranean and linked to 29% lower mortality. Napping results were ambiguous, and the article discusses how to adapt the lifestyle culturally and affordably.
one_line: A UK study using the MEDLIFE index found a Mediterranean lifestyle linked to 29% lower mortality in non-Mediterranean populations, with unclear napping effects.
key_facts: Mercedes Sotos-Prieto is an assistant professor at the Department of Preventive Medicine, Public Health and Microbiology at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid.

Researchers from the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and the Harvard Chan School of Public Health are studying adoption of the Mediterranean diet and lifestyle in non-Mediterranean populations using local products.
The Mediterranean lifestyle was linked to a 29% lower risk of mortality in both men and women.
The team created a Mediterranean lifestyle index called MEDLIFE, based on a questionnaire measuring adherence to a Mediterranean way of life.
MEDLIFE has three components: food consumption, dietary habits, and physical activity including rest, social habits, and conviviality.
The study evaluated the impact of a Mediterranean-like lifestyle over ten years in more than 110,000 participants in the UK.
All three MEDLIFE blocks were independently associated with lower mortality.
Within block 3, collective sports, limiting sedentary activities, and 6-8 hours of sleep were associated with lower mortality.
Olive oil consumption could not be included due to lack of information, so Sotos-Prieto says the Mediterranean lifestyle association is probably underestimated.
Specific napping habits were associated with higher mortality and cardiovascular disease risk, but the researchers lacked data on nap frequency and duration, and reverse causation is possible.
Previous studies found a J-shaped relationship between napping and cardiovascular disease, with short naps of 0 to 30 minutes linked to lower incident cardiovascular disease.
Sotos-Prieto suggests starting with fresh, local ingredients and realistic, sustained small goals, noting that changing habits is gradual and affordability matters.
The study is Maroto-Rodriguez J. et al., published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings (2023), using UK Biobank data.
